e.t: This Hebrew word refers to the first fruits—the earliest produce of a harvest. It is used for produce set apart in Israel’s worship and brought as an offering to God. The word appears 18 times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, especially in passages concerning harvest festivals, offerings, and giving. Its use also connects first fruits with presenting valued produce to God and with sharing it in acts of giving. Thus, it describes both the first yield of the land and its dedicated or offered use.

This Hebrew word is the personal name Ben, identifying a person in the Old Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than as a general description or action word. The name appears twice within the Hebrew Bible corpus, both in the same verse: 1 Kings 4:9. Since no broader definition or verse text is available here, its secure lexical role is to identify this individual. The surrounding passage is needed to explain the person’s particular place or responsibility in that verse.

e.t: “Baruch” functions as a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing a general quality or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it refers to named people appearing in Nehemiah and Jeremiah, including a person associated with Jeremiah’s written words and dealings. The name occurs 26 times in 24 verses, with most occurrences in Jeremiah. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding context and the person being identified.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “treasuries,” referring to places or stores set apart for valuable possessions. It presents wealth as something gathered, held, and available as a defined possession rather than as an abstract idea. The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Esther and Ezekiel. Its uses concern treasuries as objects that can be made, entered, recorded, or spoken about within the surrounding sentence.

This Hebrew word refers to a "basket," a container used to hold or carry things. It functions as a concrete noun rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs seven times across six verses, with its uses involving practical containers in different settings. Its precise use in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains a physical basket or similar vessel used for holding items.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a “familiar,” functioning as a noun for the entity associated with forbidden consultation. In its Old Testament usage, it appears in laws warning against seeking such a presence and in accounts involving people who sought its help. The word occurs 17 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 16 verses. Its connections with speech and death help show that it concerns attempted communication with the dead, rather than an ordinary human acquaintance.

This Hebrew word means “shouting,” referring to a loud vocal expression rather than a person, object, or action of movement. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Ezekiel 7:7. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence cannot be described beyond this basic lexical sense. Its role is to identify shouting in that occurrence.

This Hebrew word is a personal name identifying a king. It appears four times in the Old Testament corpus, in two verses: 2 Kings 25:27 and Jeremiah 52:31. The surrounding lexical relationships present this figure as a king and connect him with actions such as being, lifting, and reigning. Because no explicit definition or English meaning is provided, the word should be understood primarily as a name rather than as a general quality, action, or object. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “any,” serving to refer non-specifically to a person, thing, or amount rather than identifying one particular item. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible corpus, in Ezekiel 7:11. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its exact grammatical role in that sentence cannot be described further. Its basic force remains an indefinite reference: it points to something without specifying precisely which one.

This Hebrew word means “melted,” describing something changed from a solid state by heat. It functions as a descriptive word, portraying material that has softened or liquefied. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 22:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic picture is clear: something undergoing melting rather than remaining firm and solid.

e.t: Aven is a proper name, functioning as the name of a place rather than as a general descriptive word. The term appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, once in Ezekiel 30:17 and once in Amos 1:5. Because it is used as a name, its role is to identify a particular place or location in those passages, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific context.

This word is the personal name Zaavan. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears twice, once in Genesis 36:27 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:42. Both recorded English renderings preserve the name as Zaavan, so no broader ordinary meaning is established here beyond its use as a personal name. Its precise significance in either genealogy depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Abiel is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times and is rendered “Abiel.” Because the available wording identifies the name but does not provide a separate definition or explanation of its name elements, its supported meaning is simply the proper name Abiel. It appears in references from 1 Samuel and 1 Chronicles, so the surrounding verse and genealogy are needed to identify which person is intended in each occurrence.

This Hebrew word means “span,” a measure of length. It refers to a standard distance used when describing the dimensions of objects or people. In the Old Testament, it appears seven times, including descriptions of the breastpiece, Goliath’s stature, God’s measuring work, and the altar area. Its basic function is to express size or distance by this familiar measure rather than by an ordinary object’s name.

The word means “hole.” It is a Hebrew noun naming a hole, and its use is limited to two occurrences in the Old Testament, both in Isaiah. The same basic meaning appears in each occurrence, while the surrounding sentence supplies the particular setting. Thus, when readers encounter this word, they should understand a hole being referred to, not an action, person, or quality. Its two recorded uses occur in Isaiah 11:8 and Isaiah 42:22.

This Hebrew word describes something as “comely,” meaning attractive or pleasing in appearance. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Job 41:12, so its normal meaning is supported by a single scriptural use. The word functions as a descriptive term rather than naming an action or event. Its precise force in Job 41:12 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea is beauty or pleasant appearance.

This word means “fifth,” identifying the position of something as number five in an ordered sequence. It functions as an ordinal number rather than naming an object, person, or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, at Genesis 47:26. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning remains a ranking or position in a series: the fifth one. This is the only recorded occurrence in the Hebrew corpus.

This Hebrew word means “gracious.” It describes a person marked by gracious character and action, and it is used in the Old Testament particularly in descriptions of God. The word appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, including passages in Exodus, Nehemiah, Psalms, and other books. Its central idea is a gracious quality belonging to the one being described, rather than an action or object by itself.

This Hebrew word refers to an appeal for compassionate help—an asking for “mercy” or “supplication.” It describes a person turning to another with a humble request rather than making a demand. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Daniel: once rendered “mercy” and once “supplication.” Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its shared idea is a plea seeking gracious attention or relief.

This Hebrew word means “glad.” It describes a person who is glad, expressing a positive state rather than naming an object, action, or place. In its only recorded occurrence in the Hebrew Bible, it functions as a word describing the person involved. The exact force in Daniel 6:23 depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic meaning remains “glad” there.

Tebaliah is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Tebaliah.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Bible corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 26:11. As with many personal names, its broader significance is not established by the name alone; the surrounding passage is needed to explain the person’s role. The supported meaning is therefore the individual’s name, Tebaliah.

Ahian is a personal name, functioning as the name of an individual rather than as a word describing an object, action, or quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 7:19, and is rendered “Ahian.” Because it is a proper name, its role is to identify a person; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s particular place or significance in the passage.

This Hebrew verb means “defile.” It describes the act of making something defiled, so it functions as an action word rather than a name for a person, object, or place. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Song of Solomon 5:3. The surrounding verse is needed to identify precisely what is being defiled there; the word itself expresses the action of defiling.

The name appears 15 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, and Ezra. Because it functions as a person’s name rather than a descriptive word, its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the person and surrounding passage named there.

e.t: Jarah is a personal name, rendered “Jarah,” referring to a person named in an Old Testament genealogy. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in 1 Chronicles 9:42. The surrounding evidence places the name in relationships involving birth or begetting, so its role is to identify an individual within a family line. The name itself does not provide a broader ordinary meaning beyond this personal designation.

This Hebrew verb means “stand.” It describes taking or maintaining a standing position and functions as an action word in sentences. Its use can apply to people who remain in place, appear before others, or are able to withstand a situation, depending on the surrounding wording. It occurs 48 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a recurring action rather than a rare or specialized term.

It appears six times, consistently rendered “Joktan,” in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. The passages place the name within genealogical material, where it is connected with family descent and the listing of descendants. Its role is therefore to identify a person in these records.

e.t: The word means “bride,” identifying a woman in relation to marriage. It is a Hebrew noun used 34 times in the Old Testament corpus. Its function is to identify a woman within a marriage or wedding setting rather than to describe an action. The word appears across family and marriage-related passages, while its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “beams,” referring to building materials. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in 1 Kings, where the English renderings consistently identify it as “beams.” The word therefore names a physical construction element rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical sense is straightforward: beams.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Leah.” It identifies a woman in the family narratives of Genesis and later appears in Ruth. As a proper name, it functions as a person’s designation rather than as a general description, action, or quality. The name occurs 34 times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, overwhelmingly in Genesis, where it is closely associated with family history and genealogy. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical function is simply to name Leah.

This Hebrew word means “knife,” referring to a cutting instrument. It is a noun used for an object that can be carried and used in an act of cutting. The word occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including two occurrences in Genesis 22 and one each in Judges 19 and Proverbs 30. Its normal meaning remains concrete and specific: a knife, rather than a general weapon or tool. The surrounding passage is needed to explain what the knife is being used for in any particular verse.

The word’s basic sense remains focused on entry, and its meaning should be understood according to how the surrounding Hebrew sentence uses it.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Micah.” It identifies several people in the Old Testament, including individuals appearing in Judges, genealogical records, and other historical settings. The name occurs 34 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with its most frequent use in Judges. Because it functions as a name rather than a description or action, its basic meaning is identification: it tells the reader which person is being mentioned. The surrounding passage is needed to distinguish one Micah from another.

This Hebrew word is a proper name: “Mamre.” It identifies a particular place in the Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. The name appears ten times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within Genesis, and is consistently rendered “Mamre.” Its use is concentrated in passages connected with Abraham’s dwelling and the surrounding events recorded there. As a place-name, its precise significance in any individual verse comes from that verse’s surrounding context.

This Hebrew word refers to “sorrow,” expressing an experience of deep inner distress or grief. It is a noun-like term that names the painful condition itself rather than an action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 50:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is the presence of sorrow as a troubling human experience.

This Hebrew word refers to “escape”—a way of getting away from danger, pressure, or confinement. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 55:8. Because it occurs only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the wider context. Its basic sense is nevertheless clear: escape or a place of escape, expressing removal from a threatening situation.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “running,” expressing movement in progress. It describes the act or course of moving, rather than naming a person, place, or object. The word occurs five times in the Old Testament, in three verses, and its repeated rendering points to this consistent sense. Its precise emphasis—whether on the movement itself or its course—depends on the surrounding verse. It appears in 2 Samuel and Jeremiah.

This Hebrew word means “oars,” the implements used to propel a vessel through the water. It functions as a noun, naming equipment associated with a ship or boat. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Ezekiel 27:6 and Ezekiel 27:29. The surrounding language connects the word with the construction or operation of a vessel, while its basic meaning remains the oars themselves.

The Hebrew word means “soundness.” It names a condition rather than describing an action. It occurs four times in the Old Testament, in Judges, Psalms, and Isaiah. Across these uses, the word points to the state expressed by “soundness,” while the surrounding sentence determines what is being described. Its meaning is focused and consistent, though context supplies the specific application.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of being “at home,” referring to a settled place or dwelling. Its meaning is connected with home as a place where someone belongs or remains. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing this is a rare word rather than a broad, frequently repeated term. The word appears in Exodus 15:2 and Habakkuk 2:5, but understanding its precise force in either verse requires the surrounding verse and passage.

This Hebrew word is the proper name “Nahaliel,” not a general description, action, or quality. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, with both occurrences in Numbers 21:19. The English renderings consistently preserve it as “Nahaliel,” indicating that it functions as a name rather than being translated into an ordinary meaning term. Its precise significance in the verse depends on the surrounding passage, but at the word level it identifies Nahaliel.¹

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “truth.” It refers to truth as something that can characterize speech, be upheld, or be entrusted to someone. In the Old Testament, it appears 49 times, including uses connected with God’s commands, giving, and spoken testimony. The word therefore points to what is reliable and faithfully maintained, whether describing words, conduct, or a settled responsibility. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word refers to “strength,” expressing power or the capacity to stand firm. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 2:41. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the wider context. Its repeated rendering as “strength” supports this central meaning without requiring additional senses.

This Hebrew word means “brought,” describing an action in which someone or something is moved or presented into a situation. It functions as an action word rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Esther 2:20. The precise force of the action depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense centers on being brought into a stated circumstance or setting.

Sodi is a Hebrew personal name preserved in English as “Sodi.” It functions as a person’s name rather than as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 13:10. The available form identifies the person by name, but does not provide a separate lexical definition or broader meaning for the name itself.

Selah is a distinct Hebrew term preserved in English as “Selah.” It functions as an inserted word within biblical song and prayer texts rather than as an ordinary description of a person, object, or action. The term appears 74 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, overwhelmingly in Psalms and also in Habakkuk. The word occurs 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its central idea is consistent but can apply to different situations. Its precise force in any verse depends on who or what is described as prevailing.
